title: Lookalike domains and homoglyph tricks
body_md:
## Read the address, then verify the request

A link can contain a familiar name without belonging to that organisation. Your goal is to find the **host** of a complete URL and decide whether the request deserves an independent check. This is a way to slow down a rushed decision, not a guarantee that a page is safe.

A URL has a scheme (`https://`), an authority containing a host, and then a path. In `https://accounts.harborbank.co.uk.case-review.example.net/verify`, the host is `accounts.harborbank.co.uk.case-review.example.net`. The familiar bank-shaped text at the left is a subdomain under `example.net` in this synthetic address. The authority ends before `/`, `?`, `#`, or the end of the URL; the host excludes optional user information before `@` and an optional port after `:`. A name in the path, query, or page logo gives even less evidence of ownership. Use a trustworthy URL parser when the address is complicated, and verify the request independently.

## Why “last two labels” fails

For `login.harborbank.co.uk`, the public suffix is `co.uk`, so the registrable part is `harborbank.co.uk`: **three** labels. For a typical `.com` name, it is usually two. Some suffixes have still more labels, and private hosting services can have their own boundaries. The [Public Suffix List](https://publicsuffix.org/learn/) records these rules; there is no universal count-the-dots shortcut. Even a correctly parsed registrable domain only answers who may control that address. It does not prove the request is authorized, the account is secure, or the page has not been compromised.

## Similar-looking characters can name a different host

A lookalike can change the spelling of the registrable name itself: the digit `0` in the synthetic `harb0rbank.example.net` is not the letter `o` in `harborbank`. Internationalized names can also contain Unicode letters that resemble letters from another script. Browsers and registries use different safeguards, so do not assume every confusable will be displayed the same way or that a visual check will catch it. The [ICANN explanation of homograph attacks](https://www.icann.org/en/announcements/details/icann-statement-on-idn-homograph-attacks-and-request-for-public-comment-23-2-2005-en) describes the character-confusion mechanism. A strange character is a reason to stop and verify independently, not proof that every internationalized domain is malicious.

## A useful checking routine

1. Pause before opening the link. If it matters, open the service from a bookmark, its installed app, or an address you already know. Do not copy the suspect link into the address bar as a “check.”
2. If you do inspect the URL, separate the host from the path and any `@` user-info. Check its full spelling. A padlock/HTTPS means the connection can be encrypted; it is not an endorsement of the operator.
3. Treat a short link, QR code, mobile preview, or tiny address bar as incomplete evidence. Ask for the full destination or use the independent route. Do not infer safety from a brand logo or an apparently familiar subdomain.
4. A legitimate organisation may use an unfamiliar contractor or regional domain. That uncertainty calls for confirmation through its known app, website or published support channel, not an automatic “scam” verdict or a click to test it.

If you already entered credentials or a one-time code, leave the suspect page, use the genuine service through an independent route, change the affected password, review active sessions and MFA, and contact the provider through its established support channel. A URL inspection is prevention, not a substitute for incident response.

widget_config.goal: Given a suspicious link, identify its host, spot lookalike characters, and choose an independent verification route before entering anything.

blocks.title: A brand name placed inside an attacker-controlled host
blocks.situation: Synthetic: an SMS says Harbor Bank has frozen a card and points to https://harborbank.co.uk.case-review.example.net/unlock. The sender name looks familiar.
blocks.analysis: The host is harborbank.co.uk.case-review.example.net. With example.net as the registrable part in this example, the bank-shaped prefix does not establish bank ownership. The safe action is to open the bank app independently and inspect the card status there; do not enter details into this link.

blocks.title: An unfamiliar partner can still be genuine
blocks.situation: Synthetic: your bank app, opened from your phone home screen, lists a card-delivery partner at tracking.harbor-delivery.co.uk. A separate SMS also mentions that address.
blocks.analysis: The spelling alone cannot prove the partner is genuine or fake. Here the independently opened bank app supplies a trusted cross-check. Use its in-app handoff or support route; do not treat the SMS link as verified merely because it looks similar. Under the public suffix co.uk, harbor-delivery.co.uk is the registrable part, not delivery.co.uk.

blocks.title: One character changes the apparent bank name
blocks.situation: Synthetic: a message displays harb0rbank.example.net as a bank sign-in route. On a small screen, its zero can look like the letter o in Harbor Bank.
blocks.analysis: The digit 0 and the letter o are different characters. In this synthetic address the registrable part is example.net, but even a closer registered lookalike would not inherit the bank’s authority. Do not test it with credentials; open the known bank app or saved address and check the claim there. Similar-looking Unicode letters can create the same visual trap, while legitimate internationalized names also exist.

blocks.title: A delivery alert with a bank sign-in demand
blocks.setup: Synthetic scenario: a message says your new card delivery is held. It shows a link with a bank name and asks you to confirm your login before 18:00. Work through the decisions in order.

steps.prompt: The message displays https://harborbank.co.uk.card-status.example.net/confirm. What do you conclude from the address?

choices.text: The visible bank words prove the link belongs to the bank.
choices.consequence: You are ready to submit credentials on an unverified site.
choices.explanation: Those words are a prefix of a host ending in example.net.

choices.text: The host ends in example.net; the bank words alone prove nothing.
choices.consequence: You pause before opening the sign-in form.
choices.explanation: For this synthetic .net URL, example.net is the registrable part; the bank-shaped prefix is under it.

choices.text: HTTPS and the padlock prove this is the bank.
choices.consequence: You may trust an encrypted connection to the wrong operator.
choices.explanation: HTTPS protects the connection to the host; it does not identify the operator.

steps.prompt: You opened the page and see a polished bank logo, but have entered nothing. What now?

choices.text: Close the tab and open the bank app independently.
choices.consequence: You stop before exposing account information and check the claim in a known place.
choices.explanation: The page appearance cannot authenticate the operator; the app is a separate route.

choices.text: Enter only the username to see whether the page recognizes you.
choices.consequence: You have disclosed an account identifier to an unverified site.
choices.explanation: A partial login is still information an attacker can use; stop and verify outside the page.

choices.text: Click the site logo and decide from the home page design.
choices.consequence: You remain inside the same unverified site.
choices.explanation: Navigation within that site does not establish who controls it.

steps.prompt: A second link is https://login.harborbank.co.uk/account. Which domain-reading claim is sound?

choices.text: The registrable part is bank.co.uk because it is always the last two labels.
choices.consequence: You misidentify the boundary in a co.uk name.
choices.explanation: co.uk is the public suffix; the registrable part here is harborbank.co.uk.

choices.text: The registrable part is harborbank.co.uk, but that alone does not validate the request.
choices.consequence: You keep the ownership clue separate from trust in this particular message.
choices.explanation: The Public Suffix List recognizes co.uk as a suffix; independent verification is still needed.

choices.text: Any co.uk link is safe because UK domains are regulated.
choices.consequence: You skip verification on a false assumption.
choices.explanation: A suffix does not certify the sender or purpose of a link.

steps.prompt: The SMS shortens a third link, and the mobile preview hides most of its address. What is your next action?

choices.text: Open the short link and inspect the page logo.
choices.consequence: A convincing page could collect your login before you establish the destination.
choices.explanation: A logo and short link do not reveal control of the host.

choices.text: Open the bank app from your home screen and check delivery or contact support there.
choices.consequence: You can confirm the real account status without following the message.
choices.explanation: An independent route breaks the message-to-login chain.

choices.text: Forward the SMS to a friend and ask whether it looks real.
choices.consequence: You may spread the link and still lack an authoritative check.
choices.explanation: A friend can help think, but the bank app or published support channel can verify account status.

steps.prompt: Suppose you already entered a password before noticing the address. What should happen now?

choices.text: Ignore it because the page used HTTPS.
choices.explanation: HTTPS does not prevent credential theft by the site operator.

choices.text: Use the real app or known website to change the password, review sessions/MFA, and contact support.
choices.consequence: You begin containing possible account access through a trusted channel.
choices.explanation: Changing the affected credential and checking account activity addresses the exposure.

choices.text: Reply to the SMS to ask the sender to delete your password.
choices.consequence: You continue relying on the same unverified contact.
choices.explanation: The sender cannot be trusted to remediate an exposure.

blocks.debrief: The safe pattern is pause → identify the host when visible → verify through a known route → respond promptly if you already shared credentials. Reading a registrable domain is one clue, not a verdict. Do not test a suspect link by submitting information. A wrong first decision exposes a separate stop-before-entry moment; any subsequent page design remains unverified.

blocks.title: Transfer check: new addresses and requests

questions.prompt: In https://help.example.co.uk/login, what does the co.uk example show?

choices.text: The registrable part can be example.co.uk; a fixed last-two-label rule fails.
choices.explanation: Correct. co.uk is a public suffix, so the label before it is part of the registrable name.

choices.text: The registrable part must be co.uk.
choices.explanation: co.uk is the public suffix, not a name registered by this example site.

choices.text: Every address with three or more labels is malicious.
choices.explanation: Legitimate sites commonly use subdomains and multi-label suffixes.

questions.prompt: What does HTTPS establish about a login page?

choices.text: It proves the login request came from the service named in the message.
choices.explanation: Encryption does not authenticate the message sender.

choices.text: It can protect the connection to that host, but cannot prove the operator is trustworthy.
choices.explanation: Correct. Verify the request through a known route.

questions.prompt: An unfamiliar delivery partner appears inside an app you opened independently. What should you do?

choices.text: Treat the partner as automatically fake because the domain is unfamiliar.
choices.explanation: Legitimate services may use partners; confirm the handoff within the trusted app.

choices.text: Use the in-app handoff or support channel to confirm, then proceed only if it matches.
choices.explanation: Correct. The independently opened app gives better context than the SMS.

choices.text: Use the SMS link because it names the same partner.
choices.explanation: The SMS link remains unverified even if it repeats a real partner name.

questions.prompt: A URL contains bank.example.com@signin.example.net. What is the host?

choices.text: bank.example.com
choices.explanation: Text before @ is user information in the authority, not the host.

choices.text: signin.example.net
choices.explanation: Correct. The host is after @ and ends at a path slash, query, fragment, or the end of the URL.

questions.prompt: A message shows harb0rbank.example.net, with a zero in the apparent bank name. What is the useful conclusion?

choices.text: A single changed character is harmless if the page has HTTPS.
choices.explanation: HTTPS can encrypt a connection to the wrong host; it does not repair the spelling.

choices.text: Every internationalized domain is fraudulent.
choices.explanation: Internationalized names are also used legitimately; appearance alone is not a verdict.

choices.text: Treat the spelling as a warning and check the request in the known bank app or saved address.
choices.explanation: The zero changes the name, and an independent route can verify the request without exposing credentials.

widget_config.today_action: Save the bank or other high-value service in a trusted bookmark or verify its installed app. Next time a message pushes a link, open that route independently and check the request there.
widget_config.scope: General URL-reading guidance. Public suffix rules depend on the current list; account response steps vary by service and jurisdiction.
